value.overview: The Eastern Whip-poor-will is a medium-sized nocturnal bird in the nightjar family. It is best known for its repeated, whistled “whip-poor-will” song and is usually heard rather than seen. Its mottled gray, brown, and black plumage provides excellent camouflage among leaf litter and woodland shadows. The species breeds mainly in eastern North America and migrates south to winter in the southern United States, Mexico, and Central America, including rare wintering areas in Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Eastern Whip-poor-will belongs to the order Caprimulgiformes and the nightjar family Caprimulgidae. Its scientific name is Antrostomus vociferus.
value.identification: This stocky nightjar is about 22–27 cm long, with a large head, broad mouth, long pointed wings, and a short, rounded tail. The upperparts are intricately mottled in gray, brown, black, and buff, while the underparts are finely barred. A white throat patch is visible in some views, and males have broad white tips on the outer tail feathers; females usually show buffier markings. Its distinctive repeated song is often the easiest way to identify it.
value.rangeHabitat: The Eastern Whip-poor-will breeds across much of eastern North America, from southern Canada through the eastern United States. During migration and winter it uses forests, woodland edges, scrub, pine-oak habitats, and other semi-open areas with nearby perches and abundant flying insects. In Costa Rica it is not a common bird: it occurs as a casual to very rare winter resident, mainly along the Pacific slope and locally in the Central Valley, from sea level to approximately 1,200 m. Records are generally concentrated from mid-November through late March.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant with no known resident population. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon to very rare winter visitor, usually present from approximately mid-November to late March, rather than a breeding species.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs in open or semi-open forests, especially where mature woodland is mixed with clearings, sparse understory, burns, or other insect-rich openings. The species does not build a conventional nest; it lays usually two eggs directly on leaf litter or bare ground. Both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Breeding is not reliably documented for Costa Rica, where the species is considered a winter visitor rather than a resident breeder.
value.dietFeeding: The Eastern Whip-poor-will feeds mainly on flying insects, including moths, beetles, mosquitoes, and other night-flying arthropods. It usually hunts from dusk through dawn and on bright moonlit nights, launching from low perches to catch prey in the air. Its large mouth and wide gape are adaptations for aerial insect capture. In winter, including in Costa Rica, it likely forages in forest edges, clearings, scrub, and other semi-open habitats where insects are plentiful.
value.behavior: This species is primarily active at twilight and during the night. It commonly rests motionless on the ground or along low branches during daylight, relying on its cryptic plumage. Individuals are often solitary and may call repeatedly from concealed perches during the breeding season. Outside the breeding range, it is much less likely to sing, so wintering birds in Costa Rica may be detected more often by quiet observations or occasional nighttime flight than by their famous song.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered declining. Long-term monitoring has documented substantial decreases in many breeding regions, although trends vary geographically and some local populations are stable or increasing.
conservation.threats: Important threats include loss, fragmentation, and alteration of forest and open-woodland habitat; declines in insect abundance or quality; urbanization; artificial light pollution; and climate-related changes affecting migration, breeding conditions, and prey availability. Conservation concerns apply across the annual cycle, including wintering habitat in Central America. In Costa Rica, maintaining suitable forest edges, scrub, and semi-open woodland can help protect the species’ limited wintering habitat.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native forests, woodland edges, scrub, and natural clearings used by wintering nightjars. Reduce unnecessary outdoor lighting, especially near forested areas, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticide use that can reduce flying-insect prey. Support bird monitoring and habitat-protection programs in Costa Rica and across the species’ breeding and migration range. Keeping cats indoors and limiting disturbance of ground habitats can also reduce risks to nightjars and other nocturnal birds.
